Editor's note: CNN has asked its journalists across the country to offer their thoughts on how the economic crisis is affecting their cities. In this installment, Bob Crowley reports from Boston, Massachusetts. Hardware store owner Brendan Kenney says "people who have money should go out and spend it." BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) -- Brendan Kenney has seen enough bad news about the economy. "I'm also getting tired of being worried," he says. His family has been running a small hardware store in Brookline, Massachusetts, just outside Boston, for about 56 years. He says business has slowed down a little, but mostly because winter is normally the slow time of year for them. Though he hopes the stimulus plan will help his and other small businesses, he believes people shouldn't be afraid. "I think the American consumer holds a lot of power," he continues. "I think people who have money should go out and spend it." Like many in the Boston area, Kenney doesn't want to hear more discouraging stories and sees that as part of the problem. "It's just negative story after negative story, kind of creating a crisis of confidence."  Watch Boston-area reaction to the economic slump » . South of Boston, Jose Nieto, from Plainville, has his own reasons to be discouraged. Between September and October of last year, he was laid off twice. Nieto, a civil engineer who works on road construction projects, had felt fortunate. After losing his job of 14 years, he was able to find employment after only being out of work for two weeks. After being on the new job for three weeks, however, he got called into the boss's office. "I said, 'Oh, no. My God, not again.'" He was faced with looking for work in an industry that traditionally slows down in the winter months. "It's more than losing your job. It gives you a feeling of rejection," he says. Yet, Nieto feels this is a time to learn valuable lessons, especially for those who need to dip into their savings when unemployment checks don't cover all of the bills. "I think a lot of people will learn from this situation, and, going forward, they'll try to save more money." He has been trying to stay healthy, busy and positive. Passing the time working on projects in his basement workshop and taking yoga classes has helped him get through the rough spots, and his luck is turning. He was offered a job that starts in March. "It is a relief, because I'm employed," he says, "however, I'm taking a job for much less money." Nieto believes that most employers cannot afford to hire at the salaries they could offer in the past. Like Kenney's hardware store, Sue Stein's American craft gallery, also in Brookline, is not seeing any major shifts in her business, yet. "Our business has been certainly down, but not devastating," she says. Fire Opal, her gallery, sells everything from earrings to pottery to scarves, all made by artists from around the country. To keep her business healthy, she says, she is trying to make adjustments like buying less merchandise. But she is changing her approach to her customers as well. She says she tries to keep "understanding that people are having a hard time and trying to find things that are more in their price range." Like Kenney and Nieto, Stein is also trying to stay optimistic. "I think if we all are very careful," she says, "we'll sort of ride it out and then things will adjust."

**Editor’s note:** CNN has asked journalists across the country to share their perspectives on how the economic crisis is affecting their cities. In this installment, Bob Crowley reports from Boston, Massachusetts.

Hardware store owner Brendan Kenney says, “People who have money should go out and spend it.”

**BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) —** Brendan Kenney has heard enough bad news about the economy.

“I’m also getting tired of being worried,” he says.

His family has operated a small hardware store in Brookline, Massachusetts, just outside Boston, for about 56 years. He says business has slowed slightly, but attributes the decline largely to winter, which is normally the store’s slow season.

Although he hopes the stimulus plan will help his business and other small businesses, he believes people should not be afraid.

“I think the American consumer holds a lot of power,” he continues. “I think people who have money should go out and spend it.”

Like many people in the Boston area, Kenney does not want to hear any more discouraging stories and sees the steady stream of negative news as part of the problem.

“It’s just negative story after negative story, kind of creating a crisis of confidence.”

*Watch Boston-area reaction to the economic slump »*

South of Boston, Jose Nieto of Plainville has his own reasons to feel discouraged. Between September and October of last year, he was laid off twice.

Nieto, a civil engineer who works on road construction projects, initially felt fortunate. After losing the job he had held for 14 years, he found new employment after being out of work for only two weeks. However, after three weeks in the new position, he was called into his boss’s office.

“I said, ‘Oh, no. My God, not again.’”

He once again faced the prospect of looking for work in an industry that traditionally slows during the winter months.

“It’s more than losing your job. It gives you a feeling of rejection,” he says.

Still, Nieto believes this is a time to learn valuable lessons, particularly for those who must draw on their savings when unemployment checks do not cover all their bills.

“I think a lot of people will learn from this situation, and, going forward, they’ll try to save more money.”

He has tried to remain healthy, busy, and positive. Working on projects in his basement workshop and taking yoga classes have helped him through the difficult periods, and his luck is beginning to turn: He was offered a job that starts in March.

“It is a relief, because I’m employed,” he says. “However, I’m taking a job for much less money.”

Nieto believes most employers cannot afford to hire workers at the salaries they were able to offer in the past.

Like Kenney’s hardware store, Sue Stein’s American craft gallery, also in Brookline, has not yet experienced any major shifts in business.

“Our business has been certainly down, but not devastating,” she says.

Her gallery, Fire Opal, sells everything from earrings and pottery to scarves, all made by artists from around the country. To keep her business healthy, Stein says she is making adjustments, such as purchasing less merchandise. She is also changing how she approaches her customers.

She says she tries to remain mindful that “people are having a hard time” and to find items that are more within their price range.

Like Kenney and Nieto, Stein is also working to remain optimistic.

“I think if we all are very careful,” she says, “we’ll sort of ride it out and then things will adjust.”

**Editor’s note:** CNN invited reporters nationwide to describe how the financial downturn is influencing their communities. In this report, Bob Crowley examines the situation in Boston, Massachusetts.

**BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) —** Brendan Kenney, who owns a hardware store, believes consumers who can afford to make purchases should do so.

Kenney says he has grown weary of both the troubling economic headlines and the anxiety surrounding them. His family has operated a small hardware business in Brookline, just outside Boston, for roughly 56 years.

Sales have dipped slightly, he says, although he attributes much of that decline to winter, which is typically the store’s quietest season. Kenney hopes the economic stimulus package will benefit his company and other small businesses, but he argues that fear should not control people’s behavior.

In his view, American consumers have considerable influence over the economy, and those with disposable income should use it. Like many Boston-area residents, he is frustrated by the steady stream of pessimistic reports, which he believes is contributing to the situation by undermining public confidence.

*Watch reactions to the economic slowdown in the Boston area »*

In Plainville, south of Boston, Jose Nieto has more personal reasons for concern: he lost two jobs between September and October of the previous year.

Nieto, a civil engineer involved in road-building projects, initially considered himself lucky. After being laid off from a position he had held for 14 years, he found another job within two weeks. But only three weeks after starting, he was summoned to his supervisor’s office and immediately feared he was about to be dismissed again.

The second layoff forced him to search for employment in a field that normally becomes less active during winter. Nieto says job loss involves more than the disappearance of a paycheck; it can also leave a person feeling rejected.

Still, he sees the downturn as an opportunity to learn important lessons. That is especially true, he says, for people who must draw on their savings because unemployment benefits are insufficient to pay every bill. He expects many people will respond to the experience by saving more in the future.

Nieto has worked to remain active, healthy and hopeful. He has spent time completing projects in his basement workshop and attending yoga classes, both of which have helped him cope with difficult periods. His circumstances are now improving: he accepted a job scheduled to begin in March.

Although he is relieved to be employed again, the new position pays considerably less. Nieto believes many companies can no longer afford to offer the salaries they once did.

Also in Brookline, Sue Stein has not yet experienced a dramatic change at Fire Opal, her American crafts gallery. Business has clearly declined, she says, but the impact has not been disastrous.

The gallery offers products ranging from jewelry and scarves to pottery, all created by artists across the United States. To protect the business, Stein is making changes such as reducing the amount of inventory she purchases.

She has also modified how she serves customers. Recognizing that many people are struggling financially, she tries to provide items that fit within their more limited budgets.

Like Kenney and Nieto, Stein is maintaining a hopeful outlook. She believes that if everyone proceeds cautiously, they can endure the downturn until conditions eventually stabilize.

Civil engineer Jose Nieto has experienced the downturn more personally. After losing a job he had held for 14 years, he was laid off again within two months. ## Recession Squeezes Massachusetts Businesses and Workers

**BROOKLINE, Mass.** — At a neighborhood hardware store in Brookline, customers are still buying paintbrushes, furnace filters and boxes of screws. But the store’s owner says they are approaching every purchase more cautiously as the recession strains household budgets across Massachusetts.

“People are repairing things instead of replacing them,” the owner said. “They come in with a broken hinge or a worn part and ask how they can make it last another year.”

That thrift has kept some sections of the store busy, but larger sales have slowed. Contractors are ordering fewer supplies, homeowners are postponing renovations, and rising operating costs have narrowed the shop’s margins.

For an unemployed civil engineer in Plainville, the downturn is more personal. After losing his position as construction and development projects were delayed, he has spent months submitting applications and contacting former colleagues.

“You expect that an engineering degree and years of experience will provide some security,” he said. “But when projects stop, firms don’t need as many people. There are many qualified applicants competing for every opening.”

He has cut discretionary spending and taken occasional consulting assignments while looking for full-time work. His family has also postponed major purchases and is watching savings more closely.

The owner of an American craft gallery has seen similar caution among customers. The gallery sells handmade jewelry, pottery, glass and woodwork produced by artists around the country—items shoppers may admire but increasingly regard as optional.

“People still respond to the work, but they take longer to decide,” the owner said. “A customer who once bought a bowl and a pair of earrings may now choose one small piece, or leave saying they’ll think about it.”

The slowdown reaches beyond the gallery. Many craftspeople depend on sales to cover studio rent, materials and travel to exhibitions. When galleries reduce orders, independent artists feel the effects quickly.

Despite the uncertainty, all three expressed guarded optimism. The hardware store owner believes demand for practical repairs will continue. The engineer hopes public infrastructure spending will revive hiring. And the gallery owner is emphasizing affordable pieces while reminding customers that buying handmade work supports American artists.

For now, their experiences reflect different sides of the same recession: a small business adapting to frugal customers, a skilled worker searching for an opening, and a gallery trying to preserve a market for art in a period dominated by necessity.

*Editor’s note: The following is an original, fictional news-feature draft. The residents and quotations are invented for illustrative purposes; it is not published by or affiliated with CNN.*

# From cutting groceries to changing careers, three Massachusetts residents navigate an uncertain economy

### Reduced consumer spending has strained small businesses and household budgets across the state. But amid layoffs, rising costs and an unpredictable job market, some residents are finding new ways forward.

**By Staff Writer**  
**Boston, Massachusetts**

On most weekday mornings, the first thing Worcester café owner Elena Morales does is count what did not sell the day before.

A few years ago, leftover muffins and breakfast sandwiches were unusual. Now, Morales said, customers who once ordered coffee and a meal often buy only the least expensive drink — or stay home altogether.

“People still come in, but they’re making choices,” she said. “They’ll say, ‘I’d love the sandwich, but not today.’ When you hear that enough times, you understand it’s not about your food. It’s about their budget.”

Across Massachusetts, reduced consumer spending and uncertainty about the economy are forcing families and business owners to reconsider how they work, shop and plan. Higher everyday expenses have left some households with less discretionary income, while employers facing weaker demand have delayed hiring, reduced hours or eliminated positions.

The effects vary widely. Massachusetts has high-income industries and a highly educated workforce, but it is also an expensive place to live. Housing, child care, transportation and utilities can quickly consume a paycheck. For workers who lose their jobs — and for businesses that depend on their spending — even a short disruption can have lasting consequences.

Morales and two other residents described different versions of the same challenge: learning to live with less certainty. Their responses include shrinking a menu, retraining for a new career and turning a household budget into a weekly family exercise.

None expects conditions to improve overnight. All three, however, said they remain hopeful.

## A café owner learns to operate with fewer customers

Morales, 46, opened her small café in Worcester after spending years working in hotel kitchens and saving money with her husband. The shop became a neighborhood gathering place, drawing hospital employees, college students and construction crews.

Recently, she said, the morning rush has become less predictable.

Customers are not necessarily disappearing, Morales said. Instead, they are visiting less often and spending less when they do. Some bring reusable mugs for discounts. Others split pastries or skip the add-ons that once helped the café’s narrow profit margins.

The changes forced Morales to study her business in greater detail. She reduced the number of baked goods prepared each morning, negotiated smaller deliveries and removed several ingredients that were costly and frequently wasted. She also began closing an hour earlier on two weekdays.

The hardest decision was reducing shifts for two part-time employees.

“I kept putting it off because they have bills, too,” Morales said. “But if the business runs out of money, then nobody has a job.”

She has tried to avoid simply raising prices, worried that doing so would push more customers away. Instead, the café added lower-cost meal combinations and began selling family-size soups that customers can take home for dinner.

Morales also partnered with nearby organizations to provide coffee for meetings and community events. Catering orders are less frequent than everyday customer traffic, but they are larger and easier to plan around.

At home, she and her husband have paused renovations and cut back on restaurant meals. They meet every Sunday evening to review the café’s revenue and their household expenses.

The routine can be stressful, Morales said, but having a plan has made her feel less powerless.

“I can’t control the whole economy,” she said. “I can control how much food I order. I can call customers. I can make something affordable. Doing those small things keeps me moving.”

Her optimism comes partly from previous crises the business survived. Customers have also offered support in modest but meaningful ways, she said, including buying gift cards and recommending the café online.

“People don’t have unlimited money, but they want local places to stay,” Morales said. “That gives me faith.”

## After a layoff, a father rethinks what job security means

In Lowell, 38-year-old Daniel Kim begins his day at the kitchen table with a laptop, a notebook and a spreadsheet tracking every job application he has submitted.

Kim spent nearly seven years working in recruiting and operations for a technology company. When his position was eliminated, he initially treated the job search like a short interruption. He expected to find a comparable role within a few weeks.

Months later, he had completed multiple interviews without receiving an offer.

“The uncertainty was worse than the layoff itself,” Kim said. “You don’t know if you should wait for the right job, take the first thing available or completely change direction.”

Kim’s wife works as a public-school teacher, but the family had relied on both incomes to cover their mortgage, child care and payments on two cars. After the layoff, they canceled a summer trip, stopped most subscription services and began planning meals around store discounts.

They also made a decision Kim found emotionally difficult: Their younger child would attend preschool fewer days each week.

“You feel like you’re taking something away from your family,” he said. “Logically, you know you’re protecting the family’s finances. Emotionally, it feels different.”

Kim said unemployment also altered his sense of identity. In social situations, he sometimes avoided conversations about work. He worried that friends would view him differently and found himself replaying interviews, trying to determine what he had done wrong.

Counseling and a weekly job-search group helped him separate rejection from personal failure. Other members of the group reviewed résumés, practiced interview questions and shared information about employers that were still hiring.

Kim has since expanded his search beyond the technology industry. He is taking an online course in project management and has applied for positions with health care organizations, universities and local government agencies.

The transition may mean accepting a lower salary, at least initially. But Kim said he is now placing more value on stability, benefits and opportunities to learn.

“I used to think job security meant working for a successful company,” he said. “Now I think it means having skills you can take to different places.”

He has also picked up temporary consulting assignments through former colleagues. The work is inconsistent, but it has allowed the family to stretch its savings and given Kim recent projects to discuss with potential employers.

His children, ages 5 and 8, know he is looking for a new job. Kim said he and his wife try to be honest without burdening them with adult fears.

“We say, ‘Dad has more time at home right now, and we’re being careful with money,’” he said. “They don’t need to carry the anxiety.”

There have been unexpected benefits. Kim now walks his older child to school, cooks more often and volunteers at a local food pantry twice a month.

He still wants a full-time position, but he no longer describes the period solely as lost time.

“I wouldn’t have chosen this,” Kim said. “But it has shown me I can adapt, and it has reminded me that a job is important without being the only important thing about me.”

## A retiree turns careful budgeting into community support

For 67-year-old Springfield resident Margaret O’Connor, the economic slowdown has not brought a layoff. It has brought a series of smaller calculations.

O’Connor, a retired medical office administrator, lives on Social Security, a modest pension and savings. She had expected retirement to include occasional trips to visit relatives and regular dinners with friends.

Instead, she watches grocery prices closely, delays nonessential home repairs and worries about how long her savings must last.

“Nothing dramatic happens in one day,” O’Connor said. “It’s $10 more here, $20 more there. At the end of the month, you realize your cushion is smaller.”

She now shops with a strict list and visits more than one store to compare prices. Meat is less frequent, leftovers are planned rather than accidental, and the thermostat stays lower during cold weather. When her car needed repairs, she paid for them from an emergency fund but postponed replacing an aging washing machine.

O’Connor said the greatest challenge is not deprivation but uncertainty. She worries about future medical costs and whether adult children who are managing their own expenses might eventually need financial help.

She has responded by making her finances more transparent. Once a month, she reviews her accounts with her daughter and updates a document listing insurance information, recurring bills and emergency contacts.

“It was uncomfortable at first,” she said. “But pretending everything will take care of itself isn’t a plan.”

O’Connor has also found ways to maintain a social life without spending as much. She and several friends rotate hosting potluck dinners. They attend free library programs, take walks at a local park and exchange books rather than buying new ones.

The group has become an informal support network. When one friend had difficulty paying a heating bill, the others helped her identify an assistance program. O’Connor, who spent years handling paperwork in a medical office, often helps neighbors understand forms and organize documents.

She recently started volunteering at a community center, where she assists residents with appointment scheduling and basic computer tasks.

“Being useful is good for your outlook,” she said. “It gets you out of your own worries.”

O’Connor remains cautious. She checks her bank balance frequently and says she will not feel fully secure until the broader economy is more stable. Still, she believes optimism does not require ignoring risk.

“To me, optimism is not saying everything is fine,” she said. “It’s saying, ‘This is difficult, so what can we do today?’”

## Finding control in small decisions

Morales, Kim and O’Connor face different financial pressures, but each has adopted a similar strategy: focusing on decisions within reach.

For Morales, that means reducing waste and finding new customers. For Kim, it means broadening his job search and developing transferable skills. For O’Connor, it means planning carefully while building stronger ties to her community.

Their optimism remains measured. Morales does not know whether customer traffic will recover soon. Kim cannot predict when he will receive a full-time offer. O’Connor still worries that one major expense could disrupt her retirement budget.

But all three said uncertainty has made relationships more important — family members sharing financial decisions, job seekers exchanging contacts and neighbors helping one another navigate complicated systems.

Morales sees that support when regular customers return, even if they order less than before. Kim sees it in former colleagues who send job listings. O’Connor sees it around a potluck table where everyone brings what they can afford.

“Hope doesn’t mean sitting around and waiting for better news,” Kim said. “It means continuing to prepare for an opportunity, even when you don’t know when it will come.”

For now, that is how they are moving forward: cautiously, deliberately and with the belief that a downturn can narrow their options without eliminating them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
